# Ānāpānassati Sutta (MN 118 (PTS MN iii 78))

**ID:** MN 118 (PTS MN iii 78)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Ānāpānassati Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Mindfulness of Breathing
**PTS:** MN iii 78
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ānāpānassati Sutta* (MN 118; PTS MN iii 78), also known as the *Ānāpānasati Sutta*, is a major exposition on the practice of meditation in the *Majjhimanikāya* [Stanley et al. 2018]. The discourse opens with the Buddha seated among a distinguished assembly of mendicants and arahants on the Uposatha night of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, expressing deep satisfaction with their spiritual progress [Karma Sonam Palmo; Stanley et al. 2018; Anālayo 2019]. He then expounds mindfulness of breathing in sixteen sequential steps organized into four tetrads, showing how its cultivation progressively fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), which in turn fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), leading ultimately to true knowledge and liberation (*vijjā-vimutti*) [Chakma 2015; Stanley et al. 2018; Wen 2011]. The first tetrad, which focuses on the in- and out-breaths as a "body among bodies" (*kāyesu kāyaññatarā*), is directly aligned with the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and provides a foundation for both meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and insight (*vipassanā*) [Chakma 2015; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2019].

Together with the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* (DN 22), MN 118 stands as one of the central canonical reference texts for traditional meditation theory and modern mindfulness practice [McMahan 2008]. Its systematic methodology is extensively treated in later Theravāda exegetical and canonical works such as the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (*Ānāpānassatikathā*) and the *Visuddhimagga* [Chakma 2015; DharmaNexus].

 DharmaNexus machine alignments corroborate extensive internal Pali text reuse, showing that the core instructions and the enlightenment-factor sequence (§§16–40) match large segments of SN 54, SN 46 (*Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta*), MN 62, and the Vinaya *Pārājika* 3, while cross-language matches align passages with the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* and Chinese Āgamas [DharmaNexus].
